articles.title: Wyze’s latest smart bulb is also a camera
articles.summary: The latest camera from the low-cost smart home company fits into a light fixture.
articles.body: Wyze’s new security camera is attached to a lightbulb. The smart home company has devised a genius, if janky-looking, solution to illuminating your porch or patio with light while also keeping an eye on potential prowlers. The Wyze Bulb Cam ($49.98) is a motion-activated smart light and security camera that doesn’t require any power cables or batteries and is powered by a light fixture. According to Wyze, the specially designed camera can be installed directly into a compatible E26 light fixture, eliminating the need to find power outlets nearby or mess with solar panels or recharging batteries to keep your security system up and running. [Image: The Bulb Cam is IP54 rated so it can operate outdoors. The company is also selling compatible Wyze Accessory Bulbs ($16.98). These dimmable, 800-lumen, 3000-kelvin lightbulbs are IP20 rated and can pair with the Bulb Cam via Bluetooth to create a motion-activated smart lighting system. Both products are available now at Wyze’s online store. The Wyze Bulb Cam has the same lighting specs, and its camera is motion-activated. It features a 160-degree field of view, 2K resolution with wide dynamic range, and color night vision. It also has two-way audio, works over 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi, and offers local storage via an onboard microSD card (sold separately, up to 256GB). The device works with Wyze’s app, and the company offers cloud recording starting at $3 a month, which adds smart alerts for things like people, packages, and pets. [Image: The Bulb Cam offers local storage via a microSD card. Wyze says the camera is also compatible with Wyze’s new AI-powered features, including descriptive alerts that summarize motion events and its “NBD” Filter that aims to cut down on notifications — but you’ll need to pay for Wyze’s $20 a month Cam Unlimited Pro subscription. The camera and lights are compatible with Amazon Alexa, Google Home, and IFTTT. [Image: The camera can be manually adjusted, and the device fits sconces up to 7.9 inches deep. This isn’t Wyze’s first attempt at leveraging existing outdoor lighting fixtures to power cameras. The company sells a lamp socket solution for $17 that can power a Wyze Cam v3 or v4 and turns any connected bulb into a smart bulb. The Bulb Cam is slightly more elegant as it does away with the wires. While there are several no-name bulb / camera combos available on Amazon, very few established security camera companies offer this solution. Lorex recently released a 2K Wi-Fi Smart Lightbulb Camera, with the camera embedded in the bulb, which looks a little less odd, but also makes for a huge lightbulb. The Lorex can automatically rotate 360 degrees, whereas the Wyze cam can only be manually adjusted. Lorex’s bulb camera does cost more, at $70, and doesn’t have the option of local recording. [Image: The Wyze Accessory Bulbs connect via Bluetooth and are rated IP20, so need to be installed in a waterproof socket if used outdoors. The downside of connecting a security camera to an existing light fixture is that light is probably controlled by a switch, so you’ll face the same problem smart bulbs inside the house have: when someone turns off the switch, the power to the camera will be cut, as well. However, Wyze’s smart bulbs can be activated by motion via the camera or set on timers and to a schedule, so you shouldn’t need to operate them with the switch. Another issue you might run into is that a lot of exterior lighting today uses embedded LEDs and not a screw-in socket, so check yours before considering a product like this. Additionally, be aware that Wyze has suffered from several serious security and privacy issues in recent years.

articles.title: Apple is going to allow third-party app stores in Brazil, too
articles.summary: Apple is set to allow third-party app stores and for developers to use external payment systems on iOS in Brazil next year.
articles.body: Apple is set to allow third-party app stores on iOS in Brazil next year after settling with the country’s competition watchdog in a legal battle dating back to 2022, as reported by 9to5Mac. According to a machine translation of a press release from the Brazilian regulator CADE, it has approved a Term of Commitment to Termination (TCC) made by Apple that obligates the company to allow third-party app stores and let developers use external payment systems. Warnings about third-party app stores and external payment systems must also have neutral wording. Apple will be able to still charge fees, and the Brazilian publication Tecnoblog says in a machine translation that, according to CADE, those fees are: > Purchases within the App Store: > Commission of 25% (general) or 10% (special programs) > 5% fee if you use Apple’s payment system > App purchases on the App Store, but directed outside the store: > No fee if the routing involves static text (no clickable link/button) > 15% fee if the owner of the app puts a button/link and directs to payment on his own website (outside the app environment) > Alternative stores: > 5% of Core Technology Commission Apple has argued against opening up iOS on the grounds that it could compromise the platform’s security. But regulation in other countries has already forced the company to let users in Europe and Japan install third-party app stores, and in the US, Apple allows for external payment links. Apple has 105 days to put the changes into place, and if it doesn’t comply with its obligations, it could be subject to a fine of up to R$150 million (about $27 million). The company shared the following statement with 9to5Mac about the decision: > In order to comply with regulatory demands from CADE, Apple is making changes that will impact iOS apps in Brazil. While these changes will open new privacy and security risks to users, we have worked to maintain protections against some threats, including keeping in place important safeguards for younger users. These safeguards will not eliminate every risk, but they will help ensure that iOS remains the best, most secure mobile platform available in Brazil and we will continue to advocate on behalf of users and developers. Update, December 23rd: Added fee structure reported by Tecnoblog.

articles.title: Apple ordered to allow third-party app stores in Australia from 2027
articles.summary: Apple has been asked to allow competing app stores, direct app downloads and alternative payment services for users in Australia from March 1, 2027,
articles.body: Apple has been asked to allow competing app stores, direct app downloads and alternative payment services for users in Australia from March 1, 2027, following a Federal Court ruling. The court's orders follow its August 2025 finding that Apple misused its market power by limiting how users could download apps and make payments. The rules will apply to users whose Apple Account region is set to Australia, while developers enrolled in the Apple Developer Program worldwide can take part.Under the ruling, Apple must allow users to find, download, install and update apps through rival marketplaces and websites. It cannot charge users for accessing these options or create unnecessary barriers to their use.Developers must also receive the tools needed to distribute apps outside Apple's App Store on substantially the same terms as those for App Store distribution. Apple cannot penalise developers for using competing app stores or payment services.The ruling will also allow developers to offer alternative payment methods and link users to other ways to pay, including within apps distributed through the App Store. Apple cannot force developers to offer its own payment system alongside alternatives or require them to report or allow audits of transactions made through other services.Developers will also be able to offer lower prices through competing payment services without Apple blocking them.The court has placed limits on the fees Apple can charge. Apple cannot collect fees on purchases made through alternative payment services or on websites linked from apps distributed outside the App Store. For apps distributed through its own store, fees will be capped at the rate charged for payments for physical goods or services, plus any genuine and reasonable additional costs linked to digital purchases.Apple also cannot require developers to use its payment system for content bought elsewhere as a condition for allowing alternative app distribution.However, security checks will remain in place. Apps downloaded outside the App Store must undergo an automated security or privacy scan and receive notarisation from Apple or a qualified third party. Apple cannot introduce disproportionate installation barriers, and any additional security requirements for competing payment services must be necessary and proportionate.Apple will be allowed to remove or disable apps installed from outside the App Store only in specific cases, such as harmful content, genuine security risks or legal requirements. It will not have to distribute rival app stores through its own store, but it cannot ban third-party apps or alternative app stores from being preinstalled on iPhones.Apple told Reuters that it plans to appeal the ruling and ask the court to pause its enforcement, citing its intellectual property rights and App Store security.The changes will take effect at noon Melbourne time on March 1, 2027. Apple can apply to the court between February 1 and February 15, with supporting evidence, for an extension until May 3, 2027.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Can a customer buy more than two iPhones at one time: Here’s what Apple Store 'warning' in India says
articles.summary: Apple has launched iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone Duo.
articles.body: Apple has launched iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone Duo. If you are planning to order multiple iPhones for your family or hand them out as gifts this festive season, there is an important checkout barrier to keep in mind. Apple has capped iPhone purchases at a strict two units per customer on its official online store. The purchase ceiling applies across Apple’s entire active iPhone catalog – a shopper can buy two units of an identical model or mix and match two completely different devices in a single cart. The system blocks users from adding a third unit, halting the checkout process immediately.When The Times of India Tech tried to purchase three iPhone 18 Pro models, the online store flashed a message saying, “A maximum of 2 iPhone can be purchased per customer. Please adjust the total quantity of iPhone in your order before checking out.” Notably, sources told TOI Tech that this limitation is not applicable on brick-and-mortar stores.Crucially, this is neither a temporary pilot nor a policy rolled out solely for new releases like the iPhone 18 Pro series or the foldable iPhone Duo. The rule has been actively enforced on Apple's online platform for some time and governs every iPhone model currently listed for sale.How the two-unit cart limit worksThe purchase cap does not simply limit shoppers from buying multiples of a specific variant, it restricts the total number of iPhones sitting in the digital shopping bag. In everyday practice, this means:A buyer can purchase two units of the exact same iPhone model.A buyer can select two entirely different iPhone models within the same transaction.As soon as an attempt is made to add a third handset – regardless of whether it is a different model, storage tier, or colour – Apple’s checkout system stops the order and serves an explicit warning prompt.Apple has not issued an official statement for this but this may be a mechanism to prevent gray-market resellers and scalpers from cornering stock through bulk acquisitions.You use AI every day. articles.title: The world’s first triple 200-megapixel camera phone is great
articles.summary: Oppo’s Find X10 Pro Max benefits more from sensor size, dynamic range, and excellent software than sheer resolution.
articles.body: Oppo’s Find X10 Pro Max is the first phone with a triple 200-megapixel camera, which you’re likely to see as either a masterful feat of engineering or a load of hyped-up marketing nonsense. The truth is somewhere in the middle. We’ve seen 200-megapixel cameras in phones before, starting with 2022’s Moto X30 Pro. This year’s Vivo X300 Ultra was the first phone to feature two of them — with 200-megapixel main and telephoto cameras — and is still my favorite camera phone on the market. With the Find X10 Pro Max, Oppo is trying to do one better: It’s the first to use a 200-megapixel ultrawide camera too. Only the selfie camera runs at a more modest 50 megapixels. The Find X10 Pro Max’s cameras are excellent, lagging only a little behind the company’s top-tier Find X9 Ultra from earlier this year (in Oppo’s product lineup, as with rivals Xiaomi and Vivo, Pro Max phones still sit just below its top Ultra models). That’s only partly thanks to the megapixel count. The point of all those megapixels isn’t really to take 200-megapixel photos (though you can if you see fit — more on that later). Instead, like just about every phone camera from the last few years, Oppo is taking advantage of pixel-binning, which combines multiple nearby pixels into one. This gets you the best of both worlds: extra detail captured by the small, individual pixels and superior light capture from merging them together. One of the interesting changes Oppo has made is to actually reduce how much binning it uses. While most Android phones capture photos at 12 or 12.5 megapixels, regardless of their sensor resolution, the Find X10 Pro Max defaults to 26 megapixels across all three rear lenses, from 0.5x up to 9.9x zoom. That’s a similar resolution to Apple’s top iPhones, which now default to 24-megapixel shots across their 48-megapixel sensors, but still unusual for Android. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: By default, it means that shots from this phone are more detailed than on other Android rivals, and better suited to printing or cropping into. File sizes end up a little larger, of course: The Find X10 Pro Max’s 26-megapixel photos are typically 8 to 12MB, while 12.6-megapixel shots are closer to 4 to 6MB, though there’s a lot of variation. Binning to 26 megapixels rather than 12.6 has an obvious disadvantage beyond storage concerns, though: Less binning means worse light capture. In most light conditions that isn’t an issue, though, and the phone is smart enough to adapt when it becomes one, automatically dropping to 12.6 megapixels in darker scenes, sacrificing a little detail in order to maximize light when it’s in short supply. If you need high-resolution shots — or just want to force the matter and override the phone’s automatic adjustments — a high-resolution mode lets you shoot in either 50 megapixels or the full 200. Here file size balloons further, with 45 to 60MB files at the max resolution, but the 16,384 x 12,288 files are large and detailed enough to print at some size. To my surprise, I haven’t even seen much of a drop in low-light performance or dynamic range from shooting in this mode, though some difference will be inevitable in the darkest conditions. [Image: [Image: The thing with camera sensors, especially in a phone, is that resolution is only one factor — and not the most important. Sheer size matters more, which is why Oppo’s Find X9 Ultra still has an edge. The Find X10 Pro Max’s main camera uses a 1/1.3-inch-type sensor and an aperture of f/1.5, while its 3x telephoto is a little smaller at 1/1.56 inch, with a slower f/2.1 aperture. Both equivalents on the older Ultra phone use larger sensors capable of capturing more light even before pixel-binning kicks in. Only the ultrawide is improved here, with both a higher resolution and a bigger 1/1.56-inch sensor than the Ultra. But those upgrades to the ultrawide are crucial, because they help make this rear camera feel like a complete package. There’s no drop-off in resolution across the rear lenses, and only small shifts in sensor size and aperture. That means quality is consistent across the cameras, though the colors still vary a little, something I’d hope to see fine-tuned over time. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: Part of the difference likely comes down to one feature you’ll only find on the main camera: what Oppo calls “DeepPix” dynamic range. It’s similar technology to LOFIC, seen on the likes of Xiaomi’s 17 Ultra and the recent Vivo X500 Pro Max, expanding dynamic range by capturing more information from highlights. Here, it enables a 17-stop dynamic range on the main camera, keeping light sources bright and punchy in nighttime scenes without blowing them out entirely. Only a handful of phones can match this, and none that you can buy in the US. [Image: [Image: [Image: That’s just the hardware. Photos are once again boosted by tuning from Hasselblad, with some of the techniques applied in the dramatic, filmic Hasselblad Master Mode now pulled into the main camera too, primarily less-saturated colors and deeper shadows. The Master Mode still pushes the effect further if you prefer. Eighteen built-in film simulations allow more varied color profiles, and each can be tweaked further with a simple grid that adjusts tone and saturation. [Image: Each film look can be adjusted using the grid and slider at the bottom. Video has its own tricks. All three rear lenses can record at up to 120fps in 4K or 30fps in 8K, and a Pro Video mode lets you apply LUTs, record with Oppo’s O-Log2 for more post-production options, and even shoot in open gate, taking full advantage of the full sensor. Oppo’s high-end hardware accessories are back too. A teleconverter lens can be mounted on top of the telephoto lens for improved long-range photography, while a video accessory kit from Tilta includes cooling, a light, a substantial camera grip, tripod mount, polarizing filter, and more. I haven’t even spoken about the rest of the phone: a big 7,150mAh battery (even bigger outside of Europe at 8,000mAh) that lasts two days easy; a MediaTek Dimensity 9600 Pro chipset that hasn’t stuttered once; a 144Hz, 1.5K OLED display with 3,600 nits of peak brightness. Perhaps just as importantly, a design that fits all those camera specs into a relatively modest camera island, instead of the colossal ring of lenses that’s become typical on Chinese Ultra phones. [Image: The Find X10 Pro Max is launching across Europe and elsewhere, but not the US. In a flagship phone like this, none of that matters as much as the cameras. Meanwhile, Oppo’s marketing team would have you believe that in a camera like this, nothing matters as much as the megapixels. That’s not entirely true. The Find X10 Pro Max’s camera is really as good as it is because all three lenses use fairly large sensors; because the impressive Hasselblad color science has been further refined in the default camera mode; because the main lens has an almost unprecedented dynamic range for a phone. The extra megapixels are the cherry on top. Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge

articles.title: Just because Tesla’s Optimus is in production doesn’t mean it’s actually ready
articles.summary: Tesla is manufacturing humanoid robots while still working out how to make them useful, reliable, and durable enough for customers.﻿
articles.body: On Tesla’s earnings call Wednesday, CEO Elon Musk announced that the company had begun early production of its humanoid robot on its high-volume line in Fremont, California. Then he laid out what still needs work: the robot’s hands, its safety, reliability, and durability, and the artificial intelligence needed to make it a productive tool. “There’s still quite a lot of work to do with regard to the AI and the robot for it to be truly useful for open-ended tasks,” Musk said. "“At some point, there will be more humanoid robots on Earth than there are humans.”" - ELON MUSK These are substantial caveats for a product slated for volume production. Musk expects the pieces to come together around the end of 2027, when Tesla could begin delivering Optimus to outside companies, but didn’t say which or what exactly the robots would do for them. In the meantime, Tesla needs to build a fleet of robots that can practice tasks and generate training data, then feed what they learn back into the system. It also needs to integrate a new chip that Musk says will give the robots far more computing power. Tesla called the machines coming off the Fremont line its first “production-quality bots” and said its manufacturing process was suitable for a commercial product. But the company did not disclose how many robots it has produced, what tasks they can currently perform autonomously, or how often they can complete the tasks without human intervention. The announcement marks a step toward manufacturing Optimus at scale, not evidence that Tesla has a robot ready to do even the initial jobs Musk envisions — dangerous, repetitive industrial work performed around the clock — let alone become the general-purpose household machine he ultimately imagines. “You can produce them, but the software is lacking,” Ken Goldberg, a robotics professor at the University of California, Berkeley, told The Verge. “If you have a lot of hardware without the software, I think that’s a big problem.” Musk himself spent much of his discussion of Optimus explaining why investors shouldn’t expect finished robots to immediately pour out of the factory. Production will follow an S-curve, he said, with a slow, bumpy beginning. “There’s like 10,000 things that have to go right for production of the robot,” Musk said, “and it will move as fast as the slowest.” Most of the equipment for a line intended to produce a million robots annually is already in Fremont, according to Musk. But reaching a rate of 20,000 robots a week will take “at least a year, maybe a little longer,” he said. “There’s still parts of the design that are changing,” Musk said. “You’ve got to basically build up an entire gigantic global supply chain and have domestically a very, very big factory, and everything has got to work.” "“If you have a lot of hardware without the software, I think that’s a big problem.”" - KEN GOLDBERG Those production challenges are only one part of the unfinished work. A robot that can repeatedly perform a carefully defined task has a different job from a general-purpose humanoid expected to adapt to varied objects and surroundings. Musk described industrial applications as the first market for Optimus, with at-home purchases coming as the robot develops a much wider range of capabilities. Optimus is “going to do like 1,000 times more things than a car would do,” Musk said. Some of Goldberg’s more pessimistic colleagues think a truly useful humanoid robot is still 25 years away, he said. Goldberg believes the field will solve its hardest problems — including reliability, speed, and dexterity — sooner than that. But even he doesn’t expect them to be solved on Musk’s timeline. Robots have become adept at walking, running, and jumping, Goldberg said, but dexterity remains much harder. Manipulating flexible materials, such as wires and fabric, or assembling products is incredibly difficult; doing it quickly and reliably enough for real work is harder still. “I’ve been working on these problems for 40 years,” Goldberg said. “I don’t think they’re going to be solved in the next year or two.” Musk acknowledged that Tesla is ramping production before resolving Optimus’ main hardware problem: its hands. “We’re building robots that do not have perfected hands,” he said. Unlike human hands, robot hands can’t heal themselves. Yet they must withstand repeated use while remaining soft enough to handle delicate objects without damaging their sensors. “What an incredible thing the human hand is at the end of the day,” Musk said. Durability is a challenge for the rest of the robot, too. “It can’t, like, wear out after a month,” Musk said. Closing the software gap will require training data Tesla doesn’t yet have. Unlike its cars, Optimus has no vast installed base from which the company can gather information. Musk said Tesla therefore needs to build roughly 10,000 to 20,000 robots to practice tasks at what he called “Optimus Academy.” “With Optimus, we have to bootstrap it by making the robots and having them do self-play, which is really how a human learns to navigate the world,” Musk said. He compared the process to a toddler gradually mastering increasingly complex skills. “Eventually, they learn to wipe their own ass, which is a big milestone,” Musk said. “And then they learn to read and do all sorts of things.” Goldberg described learning through self-play as a hypothesis whose success in software doesn’t establish that it will work as well in physical hardware. “When you get into hardware, it’s not so clear,” he said. Tesla is also waiting on hardware that has yet to be integrated. Musk said he hopes to put the company’s AI5 chip into Optimus around April 2027, providing roughly 10 times the computing power of AI4. He expects the new chip, improved software, and mechanical refinements to come together before customer deliveries. If all that works, Musk expects Optimus will eventually have a hand in its own production. “The Optimus robots will build the future Optimus robots,” he said, describing a self-reinforcing production loop that would grow “extremely fast.” “At some point, there will be more humanoid robots on Earth than there are humans,” Musk predicted. Before then, Musk promised a video within a month or two showing Optimus performing tasks that aren’t preprogrammed. He criticized humanoid demonstrations that look impressive but wouldn’t translate into useful real-world performance. “If you actually try to use that humanoid robot in the real world, you would have a lot of trouble,” he said. “It wouldn’t work, basically.” Goldberg calls the problem “video emptor.” A video might show the one successful attempt out of a thousand, he said, hide a person controlling the robot offscreen, or depend on a precisely arranged setting. In robotics labs, task success rates have stalled at around 70 to 80 percent, Goldberg said. “That’s not acceptable for real industry.” Musk remains convinced Optimus will become “the biggest product on Earth.” While Tesla’s announcement brings it closer to manufacturing Optimus in large numbers, building a robot customers can depend on – and actually use – remains a separate milestone.

articles.title: Birdbuddy’s Nook is a compact smart bird feeder for small spaces and budgets
articles.summary: The new smart bird feeders Birdbuddy announced earlier this year are now available, including the compact and budget-friendly Nook.
articles.body: Birdbuddy is finally launching the new smart bird feeders it originally announced at CES 2026 earlier this year, but with new names. The Birdbuddy 2 Mini is now called the Birdbuddy Nook, and it is designed to be a smaller and more affordable option the company describes as its “most accessible smart bird feeder yet.” The flagship Birdbuddy 2 has been renamed the Birdbuddy Home and delivers upgrades like a redesigned camera with a wider field of view and integrated solar panels. Both models are now available through Birdbuddy’s online store while some configurations will be available at other retailers later this month. The Birdbuddy Nook starts at $99 and features a redesigned circular 2K HDR camera with a 135-degree field of view. The camera wakes up the moment a bird lands to help ensure visits are captured. The camera can shoot in landscape or portrait orientations, making it easier to share videos and images on social media, while the AI-powered Birdbuddy app identifies exactly what species is visiting. [Product: Birdbuddy Nook | The Nook’s 3.8-cup seed reservoir may need frequent refills if a lot of birds regularly stop by, but you can avoid frequent battery charges by upgrading to the $159 Nook Solar, which adds a solar panel to the roof. For an extra $40 on top of that, the $199 Nook Extended Edition includes a larger perch to accommodate more birds. [Image: The Birdbuddy Home comes standard with two solar panels on the roof to help extend battery life. The $219 Birdbuddy Home uses the same 2K HDR camera with a 135-degree field of view as the Nook, but in a larger feeder designed to require less maintenance. It has a six-cup seed reservoir and comes with a pair of solar panels on top to help keep the battery charged, assuming the feeder’s installed somewhere with adequate sun exposure. The Home also has a built-in perch extender to accommodate more visitors, dual-band Wi-Fi, and an upgraded mic that can help the mobile app more accurately identify a species through its birdsong.

articles.title: Insta360 launches a cheaper version of its wireless mics with color screens
articles.summary: Insta360’s new Mic skips some of the Mic Pro’s premium features but still includes a color screen you can customize with logos or photos.
articles.body: Following the launch of its wireless Mic Pro system last May featuring built-in color E Ink screens for custom branding and an array of three microphones to emulate different pickup patterns, Insta360 has announced a cheaper alternative that skips a few features many content creators might not miss. The new Insta360 Mic sits between the company’s Mic Pro and the budget-friendly Mic Air, which uses much smaller screenless transmitters. While the Mic Pro is priced at $329.99 for a kit that includes two microphone transmitters, one wireless receiver, and a charging case, the Insta360 Mic costs $249.99 for a similar bundle. Insta360 sells the microphones individually since they can directly connect to smartphones and many of the company’s cameras (including the X6, X5, and Luna Ultra) over Bluetooth. The Mic Pro transmitter on its own costs $99.99, while the new Insta360 Mic is $79.99. [Image: The Insta360 Mic is available in bundles that include two transmitters, a wireless receiver, and a charging case. The design and functionality of the Insta360 Mic is very similar to the Mic Pro. It has the same 1.22-inch, six-color E Ink display on the front that can be customized with logos, photos, or solid colors to help it blend into clothing. The transmitters have a range of up to 400 meters when paired with Insta360’s wireless receiver that can connect to professional cameras, laptops, or other recording devices using a built-in USB-C connector. The Insta360 Mic also features AI-powered noise canceling to reduce background noise and automatic gain control modes that adjust recording levels on the fly to help prevent clipping if things suddenly get too loud. [Product: Insta360 Mic | So what are you missing out on when choosing the cheaper Insta360 Mic? The biggest downgrade is that the transmitters have just a single mic instead of the triple mic array in the Mic Pro, so you cannot select from multiple pickup patterns; omnidirectional is the only option. However, that simplified hardware makes the transmitters slightly lighter than the Mic Pro’s — 19.4 grams compared with 19.7 grams — and battery life increases from up to 10 hours to up to 13 hours, which can be boosted to 34 hours with the charging case. The Mic Pro’s transmitters come with 32GB of built-in storage for creating a backup recording. The Insta360 Mic transmitters don’t have any built-in storage, but you can enable backup recording by sticking a microSD card inside each one. As with the lighter design and improved battery life, the microSD option also feels like an upgrade for the Insta360 Mic if you want more than 32GB of storage.

articles.title: Googlebooks just aren’t ready
articles.summary: Googlebooks review: Acer, Asus, Dell, HP, and Lenovo made some good laptop hardware, but Google’s OS is a dealbreaker in its current state.
articles.body: Every Googlebook laptop we’ve tested so far has great hardware. The problem is the software. While Googlebook OS has exciting ideas for how a laptop and phone can work together, right now it’s mostly a frustrating experience filled with annoying bugs and lackluster app support. It often feels like using an Android tablet with a keyboard and trackpad grafted on, rather than a cohesive laptop OS. It’s too bad, because those keyboards and trackpads — and pretty much all the laptops’ hardware components — are great. Frankly, they should be. The cheapest is $900, a price where you start to expect quality processors, metal builds, higher-quality displays, good speakers, and great keyboards and trackpads (even haptic ones in some cases). The Googlebooks have those covered, and they also have very good battery life and at least 16GB of RAM. Google wanted Googlebooks to feel premium, and HP, Acer, Lenovo, Dell, and Asus all delivered. It’s Google’s software that needs to catch up. In their current state, we don’t recommend you buy any of them. But it’s worth reviewing the hardware to determine which shows the most promise if the software one day improves — or if crafty modders manage to install other operating systems. Since the software is the same on all Googlebooks (save for some preinstalled manufacturer apps), and we’ve already covered that software at length, we’re strictly talking about Googlebook hardware here. The scores, however, cover hardware and software as they stand today. Brace yourself — the scores are bad. If you’re a dedicated Google user or Pixel fan and you really want to be an early adopter / paying beta tester — or if you’re just here for some schadenfreude — here are our collective thoughts on each and every Googlebook. [Product: Acer Googlebook 14 | The Acer Googlebook 14 is the only 2-in-1 convertible of the bunch, and it’s one of the nicest-feeling and -looking Acers I’ve ever used at this price. It’s light, with a sturdy metal chassis and a great 2880 x 1800 / 120Hz OLED touchscreen with stylus support. I find 2-in-1s pretty handy, even if they look clunkier than tablets like a Microsoft Surface Pro or an iPad with a keyboard case, but Googlebook OS doesn’t yet support portrait orientation, which limits the Acer’s stylus potential. Like all Googlebooks, the Acer has an Auto-Rotate toggle in settings, but it only flips the orientation 180 degrees — a strange oversight. The speakers don’t have a lot of bass, and they can get muffled in tablet mode depending on how you hold the laptop, but they’re decent and sound balanced overall. The webcam is a slight weak point, as colors and contrast are a touch drab. But nothing here is bad. This isn’t like some of the Acer Aspires or Swifts I’ve tested in the past where you had to deal with a terrible screen and shoddy build quality for the sake of a good chip. It’s just an all-around nice package. That extends to the battery life, which lasted me eight to nine hours of light-to-mixed usage. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: If this was running Windows or a proper Linux distro with the same hardware and price, it’d be a rare bright spot in our ongoing RAMageddon hellscape. But thanks to Googlebook OS, it’s not. And an Acer rep told us its $900 launch price is only available for a limited time. That might sound like an incentive to buy one before a price increase, but please allow me to tap the “Don’t buy it now for what it might do later” sign. Actually, picture me tapping it as you read this whole article. — Antonio G. Di Benedetto, Laptop Reviewer [Product: Dell XPS Googlebook | Here’s my theory: If Googlebooks are going to work anytime soon, they’re going to work as secondary computers. Maybe they don’t need to replace your primary work machine if they can instead be light, fast, simple, and fun to use. (Yes, I agree that $900 or more is a lot to pay for this kind of device, but hey, iPads pull it off!) I already see glimmers of possibility here, even through the bugs of Googlebook OS. “A Chromebook, but also it runs all my apps” is not a bad pitch for an off-day computer. That’s why, of all the available Googlebooks, the Dell XPS Googlebook makes the most sense to me. At 2.2 pounds, with a 13.4-inch screen, and starting at $999, it’s one of the smallest and lightest Googlebooks available. (And unlike the cheaper Acer Googlebook 14, it doesn’t offer a bunch of flippy tablet modes that don’t really work.) Like the other models we’ve tested, it’s a lovely piece of high-end hardware; I love the keyboard and trackpad, I appreciate that I can open the thing with one hand, and the Qualcomm chip inside does its job fine for all my practical purposes. The battery got me through a full day of travel and then some. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: My only real complaint is with the anti-glare coating on the display, which does help tamp down reflections but also creates that slight rainbow-shimmer effect that makes the screen appear a little less sharp and clear. The coating also dims the screen a bit — I’ve used the XPS Googlebook mostly at max brightness, just to get it up to normal. I am generally extremely in favor of these matte displays, but I’d trade the XPS Googlebook’s for a glossy one in a heartbeat. As we keep saying, there’s simply no way around the fact that Googlebook OS isn’t ready. Google is fixing and improving it quickly (adding the ability to run any website as an app was a big win), but I can’t get past the apps that don’t work properly with a keyboard, don’t work on this size screen at all, or simply don’t exist on Googlebook OS (bring back Linux apps, now!). If you’re in the market for an overpriced second computer and you want easy access to Google Messages and your Drive files, a Googlebook might be exactly what you need. Someday. Maybe by then Dell will have fixed the screen. — David Pierce, Editor at Large [Product: HP Googlebook 14 | HP’s Googlebook 14 is more proof that of all the problems facing these early Googlebook models, the hardware isn’t one of them. Starting from $1,199.99, this Googlebook is about the same size and weight as a MacBook Air 13, despite fitting in a larger 14-inch display. It’s a great panel, too: a 2880 x 1800 resolution, 120Hz, OLED touchscreen with a slim bezel, good viewing angles, and punchy brightness. The Snapdragon X Elite chip has proved reliable so far (and for what it’s worth, my Asus model with an Intel chip has been solid too, despite early concerns), with 16GB of RAM and the option to bump memory up to 32GB and storage as high as 1TB, but I haven’t pushed it through anything more demanding than image editing in the infuriating mobile versions of Lightroom and Photoshop. The body is mostly metal, so the whole thing feels tough and solid. The keyboard’s comfortable and the haptic trackpad expansive, and the privacy shutter on the webcam is always a welcome touch. There are only two USB-C ports and a headphone jack, so grab one of the other Googlebooks if you know you need HDMI or USB-A. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: I’m a fan of the Googlebook-specific hardware touches too, which you’ll find across the lineup. I’m already building the habit of using the Caps Lock key for its Quick Insert function instead, with easy access to features like the clipboard, emoji, and Rambler dictation — though the latter gets its own dedicated function key too. It’s joined by keys for the classic Android navigation buttons and a shortcut for some flexible screenshot and screen recording options. The Glowbar is a little less impressive; it’s a cute design but doesn’t actually do very much, and since it’s on the lid you’ll rarely see it in action anyway. From the hardware side this feels like a $1,200 laptop through and through — it’s the software where we still have questions. — Dominic Preston, News Editor [Product: Asus Googlebook 14 | Asus’ entry in the first slate of Googlebooks was able to keep up with me better than I expected, with solid hardware that helped soften the blow of software frustrations. At $1,299, the Asus Googlebook 14 is the priciest of the first five Googlebooks. The base configuration has an Intel Core Ultra 5 325 CPU, 16GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage (you can also get the 512GB model for the same price at Best Buy). I rarely felt like I was pushing those specs to their limit — the Asus got pretty toasty when I was running games on it, but that’s true of just about any laptop. It breezed through things like managing a dozen or more Chrome tabs and hopping between a few different apps at once. Asus says the 70Wh battery lasts up to 18 hours, and while I didn’t get quite that long, I didn’t have trouble getting through a typical day without charging. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: One major plus is the Asus’ wealth of ports: two USB-C, two USB-A, a headphone jack, and even HDMI. That’s more than most of the other Googlebooks have, or my MacBook for that matter. I was able to hook up the Asus to my monitor, keyboard, mouse, and a wired controller without needing a USB-C hub or a docking station. I mainly used the Asus without my external monitor, though, largely because it has a fantastic keyboard — it’s satisfyingly clicky with good key travel and tactile feedback. The 14-inch OLED (2880 x 1800) display doesn’t disappoint, either. It has a 120Hz refresh rate and a nice matte finish. The few games that ran well on the Asus, like the Android version of Dredge, looked great. The Asus Googlebook 14 has some real highs, but the current Googlebook OS experience makes it a tough sell at $1,299. For the same price, you could get the 13-inch M5 MacBook Air with similar specs or, for $100 more, you could also get Asus’ new Windows ExpertBook A7. — Stevie Bonifield, News Writer [Product: Lenovo Googlebook 15 | The $1,099 Lenovo Googlebook 15 is the largest of the launch lineup, and it’s low-key my favorite. I love a bigger screen, especially in a lightweight laptop. At around 2.8 pounds / 1.27kg, the Lenovo Googlebook is nearly half a pound lighter than Apple’s 15-inch MacBook Air. It’s not as thin or nice as a MacBook Air, but it makes up for that with more ports (HDMI 2.1, two USB-C, and one USB-A). It also has a bright 2880 x 1800 / 120Hz OLED display and a large haptic trackpad that feels and sounds like a tight drum when you click it. Despite that sizable OLED, the battery easily lasted me an eight-hour workday of navigating Chrome tabs with a handful of extra apps like Apple Music and Signal running. And its light gray color and satiny finish is just charming. Of the three Googlebooks I’ve tested (I tried the HP as well), this has been the one I used the most because of that larger screen and satisfying trackpad. The speakers are good too, with a touch of stereo separation due to the laptop’s size, and they get surprisingly loud. On the other hand, the keyboard is only fine. It’s got a nice clacky feel, but the keycaps are slightly wobbly, and overall it lacks the tight, satisfying tactility of other Lenovo laptop keyboards (like ThinkPads). And while I love this laptop’s off-white color, the bright white keyboard backlight sometimes makes the legends harder to see unless you’re actually in a dark space (this is one place RGB backlighting would actually help). [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: Also included with the Lenovo Googlebook 15 (at least, if you buy it directly from Lenovo or Google) is an AI Mouse. Uhh. It’s a Bluetooth mouse. It’s got a light-up button for launching Gemini. That’s about all that makes it an “AI Mouse.” Having a Glowbar that actually faces you seems like a nice idea, but just like the ones built into the lid of every Googlebook, the one on the mouse doesn’t do much. You can pick different lighting colors and patterns in the preinstalled Lenovo Vantage app, and the Glowbar does a brief colorful flourish when you summon Gemini — but that’s about it. It’s just a fine ergonomic mouse that matches this fine laptop hardware. And that’s the story with every Googlebook so far: The hardware is fine, and even great. But until the software is worthy of the hardware, that’s just not good enough. — Antonio G. Di Benedetto, Laptop Reviewer

articles.title: The Atari VCS saga will come to an end next year when its software store closes
articles.summary: Atari announced that in early 2027 it will be shutting down the Atari VCS’ software store, but the retro console will still be able play games.
articles.body: Following a decade-long saga of delays, name changes, and Atari having to assure backers of a crowdfunding campaign that its retro console wasn’t doomed, the Atari VCS platform is being retired early next year. On February 1st, 2027, the Atari VCS software store is shutting down, according to an announcement posted to the Atari Club Discord and shared by Tom’s Hardware. With a design loosely inspired by the original Atari 2600 — minus a cartridge slot — the VCS was a Linux-based, AMD-powered mini PC that could emulate a large collection of pre-loaded classic Atari games, but its functionality could be expanded through an online software store that included access to streaming platforms and, in recent years, game streaming platforms like Xbox Cloud Gaming and Nvidia GeForce Now. Atari VCS owners will still be able to download and add software to their libraries through Atari’s official online store up until January 31st, 2027. After that, the store will officially shut down, but previously downloaded apps and games will still be usable. Atari says that following the store’s closure it plans to “make an OS update available that allows you to migrate all functionality to your local machine, removing any dependencies on Atari infrastructure for authentication and software.” The company also plans to release an Atari Home Brew app allowing owners to continue to add new games to their console’s library shared to the community by third-party developers who still want to develop and support the VCS.

articles.title: Apple will label apps that are ‘Made for iPhone Duo’
articles.summary: Apple says it will label apps if they’re optimized for its new foldable. The “Made for iPhone Duo” badge will appear across the App Store on apps like Netflix, Prime Video, Microsoft Word, Instagram, and more.
articles.body: Apple is rolling out a new badge in the App Store to indicate whether an app is optimized for its new foldable. The new “Made for iPhone Duo” badge will appear across apps and games that work with the device’s extra screen real estate. Though Apple doesn’t include an image of what this badge might look like, it highlighted some of the ways apps are taking advantage of the Duo’s inner and outer screens. Netflix, for example, will display shows and movies that take up the whole inner display, while allowing you to watch its feed of short-form clips on the outside. Amazon’s Prime Video will let you watch shows and movies with the Duo partially folded, with the content on top and details about the cast on the bottom. [Image: Prime Video can show details about the cast while you watch a movie with the Duo partially folded. Meanwhile, Apple says Microsoft Word and Outlook will offer a “desktop-class” experience on the Duo, with Word placing its formatting tools alongside a document, and Outlook displaying your inbox next to a full email. Zoom can also display a video conference alongside shared content across the iPhone Duo’s inner screen. Other apps optimized for the Duo include Paramount Plus, NYT Cooking, Yelp, Lyft, and United Airlines. But, as The Verge’s Nilay Patel found during his Duo testing, some apps “optimized” for the device, like Instagram, still have some bugs. Apple says it’s going to launch editorial collections for the iPhone Duo on Friday, “with additional app updates rolling out throughout the year.” The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 and launches on Friday, with “limited” quantities available on a walk-in basis.

articles.title: Medicaid billing abuse deprives autistic kids of therapy and taxpayers of trust
articles.summary: Runaway applied behavior analysis spending exposes the moral hazard at the heart of Medicaid’s financing architecture.
articles.body:
News stories involving fraudulent government payments and the widespread misuse of tax dollars have become all too common. The latest scandal involves Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program, or CHIP, two critical safety-net programs meant to serve society’s most vulnerable.

Government spending on applied behavior analysis therapy for children with autism has exploded in recent years. Unfortunately, federal investigations have revealed that this higher spending increasingly reflects rampant billing abuse by unscrupulous providers, leaving taxpayers to foot the bill.

The numbers just don’t add up. According to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, Medicaid and CHIP spending on applied behavior analysis therapy jumped from $2 billion in 2021 to over $10 billion by 2025. That’s more than a 400 percent increase , despite the fact that the number of children receiving an autism diagnosis only grew by 67 percent.

State-level data are just as jarring. In Minnesota , Medicaid spending on autism therapy skyrocketed from under $700,000 in 2018 to over $342 million by 2024, while in North Carolina, outlays grew from $1.9 million in 2020 to over $505 million in 2025. Indiana offers an especially egregious example. In 2023, the Hoosier State paid a single provider $29 million for therapy services covering just 84 patients, about $340,000 per child.

Today, autism treatment is one of the fastest-growing categories of Medicaid spending.

Federal officials took notice. Investigators released audits for just four states — Indiana, Colorado, Maine and Wisconsin and found hundreds of millions of dollars in improper disbursements, including payments made to ineligible recipients, payments in the wrong amount and payments made without proper documentation. Officials have since recommended that these state governments return roughly $123 million in misspent federal funds.

None of the four states had performed a statewide post-payment review of these Medicaid fee-for-service claims. Colorado’s example makes this oversight failure particularly appalling. Federal auditors determined that every single one of the 100 sampled enrollee months contained potentially improper payments. Providers were found to be charging Medicaid for services delivered by staff without proper credentials and, in some cases, even billing naps and group recreation as one-on-one therapy.

The problem goes far beyond lax oversight and billing errors. Earlier this year, the Department of Justice filed criminal charges in what it alleges was a $46 million Medicaid fraud scheme that involved billing for services that were never delivered and using falsified diagnoses.

This isn’t just about bad actors abusing the healthcare system. Runaway applied behavior analysis spending exposes the moral hazard at the heart of Medicaid’s financing architecture. Since the program is structured as an open-ended entitlement, state Medicaid spending automatically triggers federal matching funds. However, because states don’t fully fund their Medicaid programs, they have little incentive to control spending and prevent abuse.

Fortunately, the government is taking steps to address runaway applied behavior analysis therapy spending. The agency recently unveiled a toolkit that offers states practical advice on verifying provider qualifications and ensuring tax dollars fund only clinically appropriate care. As part of a broader effort to combat fraud, federal health officials are also developing the Comprehensive Regulations to Uncover Suspicious Healthcare rule, which seeks to leverage artificial intelligence to stop improper or fraudulent payments in real time.

Congress is acting, too. House Republicans recently introduced the Anti-Fraud Fund Act of 2026 , which would allocate billions of dollars to federal investigators and prosecutors to proactively fight fraud in federal health programs. But beefed-up enforcement can only go so far.

As long as Medicaid’s open-ended entitlement status lets states shift costs to federal taxpayers, incentives to limit fraud and improper payments will remain weak. If Congress wants to tackle the root of the problem, it should consider reforming Medicaid into a block grant, which would give states a fixed amount of money instead of an open-ended federal match.

Applied behavior analysis therapy is a vital tool to help children with autism flourish, and Medicare and Medicaid administrator Mehmet Oz illustrated the stakes perfectly when he affirmed that “every dollar lost to fraud or waste is a dollar that cannot reach a child who genuinely needs it.”

Policymakers must ensure Medicaid remains a lifeline for vulnerable children — not a vehicle for wasteful spending.

Alex Ciccone is Policy and Government Affairs manager at National Taxpayers Union.

articles.title: Coolpad’s new $150 Android phone has a wider screen like the iPhone Duo, but doesn’t fold
articles.summary: Coolpad’s new Cool X Wide has a wider display with a 16:10 aspect ratio making it look like recent foldables, but it’s a budget-friendly Android slab phone.
articles.body: The design of widescreen folding phones like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, Huawei Pura X View, and now the iPhone Duo, is starting to influence traditional slab phones. Similar to the Huawei Pura X View that launched in China in August, the new Coolpad Cool X Wide has a much wider screen than what’s typically seen in non-folding phones. The screen real estate is more on par with what you get from a tiny tablet, or what the iPhone Duo and Galaxy Z Fold 8 offer when closed, minus huge price tags, budget-stressing repair costs, and inevitable screen creases. The Coolpad Cool X Wide is now available for preorder through JD.com in China for 999 Chinese Yuan, or around $150, in black, red, or white color options. Shipping is expected to start on November 8th. So while its display is reminiscent of the recent crop of pricey foldables, this is a budget Android phone through and through. It’s powered by a MediaTek Helio G99 processor with 8GB of RAM and 128GB of storage. You can bump that to 256GB of storage which pushes the price to around $180, or increase the RAM to 12GB for around $209. [Image: The Coolpad Cool X wide looks more like a tiny tablet than a smartphone. The Cool X Wide’s 6.38-inch display has a 16:10 aspect ratio with refresh rates up to 90Hz and a 1,158x720 resolution. There’s also a 50-megapixel main camera on the back and a 4,600mAh battery. It comes with Android 16 out of the box, but the phone’s processor limits its connectivity to only 4G networks, as Android Authority points out. If you’re wondering how a device with a 16:10 screen will feel in hand, the Cool X Wide is nearly exactly as tall as the iPhone 18 Pro, but while Apple’s latest is 2.83 inches wide, the new Coolpad is 3.72 inches.

articles.title: Coolfly’s solar-powered Aura Smart Bird Feeder is nearly 50 percent off

articles.body: I’m not sure when bird-watching became so popular, but it seems everybody’s getting into it these days. If you want to see what all the fuss is about without leaving your couch, both Coolfly and Birdfy are discounting their camera-equipped bird feeders for a limited time. Right now, you can buy Coolfy’s Aura Smart Bird Feeder for $149.90 ($140 off) or the Birdfy Feeder from Amazon or Birdfy for $109.99 ($90 off). You can also add a solar panel to the latter for an extra $20 from Birdfy, or grab both the panel and lifetime AI-powered bird identification from Amazon or Birdfy for $149.99 ($110 off). [Product: Aura Smart Bird Feeder | [Product: Birdfy Feeder | My colleague Jennifer Pattison Tuohy called the Aura Smart Bird Feeder an impressive package, praising its large seed hopper, exceptional battery life, and dual solar panels. She also liked its unique side-mounted camera, which provides a more natural, wider view of birds than many other smart feeders. It can capture up to 2.5K video with a 150-degree field of view and offers full-color night vision, cloud and local storage, and AI-powered identification of more than 10,000 bird species, all without a subscription. Birdfy’s feeder offers many of the same perks for less, including 2K video, night vision, and AI-powered identification of more than 6,000 bird species. It also lets you watch visiting birds on your phone, set up notifications for when they stop by, and access recordings via the cloud. Unlike the Aura, however, solar charging and lifetime AI identification aren’t included by default, with a subscription running $49.99 a year if you don’t purchase a bundle. It also supports up to 100W USB-C passthrough charging, so you can keep your laptop or tablet powered while using your connected devices. * Govee’s Smart Curtain Lights 2 are on sale at Amazon starting at $99.99 ($50 off), which is the best price we’ve seen this year and only $20 shy of their all-time low. The water-resistant curtain lights feature 520 individually controlled LEDs that can be programmed to display colorful patterns, animated GIFs, and even your own images. They also offer more than 200 preset lighting effects, sync with music, and can be controlled via any major smart home platform.

articles.title: You could just get a refurbished Samsung phone on Amazon
articles.summary: Samsung is offering certified renewed phones on Amazon now, but it isn’t the only way to get a cheaper phone.
articles.body: I recently bought a used Galaxy phone, and now Samsung is leaning into that market on Amazon after raising prices on its newest phones. Its certified renewed phones are available on Amazon for the first time, with a new battery and a one-year warranty. They currently start at $489 for the Galaxy S24 FE with 128GB of storage, significantly less than its $649 launch price, or $699 for the current-gen S26 FE. I got that exact same phone in August after cracking the screen on my Nothing CMF Phone 1. But my used 128GB Galaxy S24 FE cost $329 on Back Market, over $100 less than the certified renewed one Samsung is offering. I’ve gone with preowned phones a couple of times now since I don’t use my phone for anything that justifies paying hundreds more for a new one. I’d rather not go into debt for a new phone with a buy-now-pay-later program, either, or lease-to-own setups like Apple’s Upgrade program. My used S24 FE looks new, still has five more years of OS updates, and has been working great so far. These aren’t the only ways to get a used phone without looking around on Facebook Marketplace or eBay either; Apple and Google offer used phones on their online stores at a discount, for example. Samsung’s perks for its certified renewed phones are nice, especially the new battery, but you can find those elsewhere, too. My S24 FE came with Back Market’s one-year warranty. It didn’t come with a new battery, but I haven’t had trouble getting through a couple of days on a single charge. Some third-party refurbished phones come with new batteries installed, but you can also do a DIY battery replacement. Even if I had paid to have my phone’s battery professionally replaced, it would still have cost less in total than Samsung’s $489 price for the same pre-owned phone.

That said, Woot says they’re in “pristine condition, with essentially no visible signs of use.” If you’re still interested, the savings should be worth it. The most affordable option is the Magic Keyboard for the 13-inch iPad Air (M2, M3, M4 versions supported). Originally $319, and selling for that price at most retailers, you can nab one in white for just $129. [Product: Apple Magic Keyboard Case for iPad Pro (M4, M5) | Each Magic Keyboard essentially turns your iPad into a MacBook, of sorts, complete with a trackpad, aluminum design, and a function row of keys. It magnetically attaches to the back of your iPad, and gets power via its pogo pins, keeping the tablet’s USB-C port free for you to plug in accessories. The keyboard accessory features a USB-C port in its cantilevered double-hinged design for charging your iPad (this port doesn’t allow data passthrough, just power). The stand lets you make easy adjustments to the viewing angle of your iPad, which is great if you’re trying to avoid glare.

articles.title: Microsoft shuts down its beloved maker space
articles.summary: Microsoft is closing The Garage, its internal maker spaces used for hackathons and employee experiments. The spaces have existed for 17 years.
articles.body: Microsoft is closing down The Garage, a set of popular maker spaces where employees worked on experimental projects and collaborated on surprising new apps and hardware during the company’s annual hackathon events. “We’re winding down The Garage program as a centralized function,” says Microsoft in an internal FAQ to employees, seen by Notepad. “We will continue to explore new ways to help employees build skills, collaborate across boundaries, and bring a hacker mindset to their work.” GeekWire first reported on The Garage’s closure. The main Garage space was located at Microsoft’s Redmond, Washington, campus and served as the central hub for around 15 Garage locations across the US, Canada, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia. Microsoft employees could use it to experiment with prototypes, build hardware, and even turn hobbies into full Microsoft products. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella regularly attended Garage hackathons, giving employees a chance to showcase their projects and attract the attention of senior executives. Many apps and services have emerged from The Garage over its 17-year history, including the AI-powered Seeing AI app that describes objects and text to people who are blind or have low vision. It was born out of a 2015 hackathon event and shipped 10 years ago. Microsoft employee Tuong Do used The Garage to develop Mouse Without Borders in his spare time, working on it during evenings and weekends. The app is still available today and lets you control up to four PCs with a single mouse and keyboard. Microsoft employees have also used The Garage to develop new learning tools and accessibility features for Word, Microsoft Edge, and PowerPoint. I would point you to the Microsoft Garage hall of fame for a list of all the top projects, but Microsoft has removed the website — erasing the rich history of its employee-led workshop. One of the most famous success stories of The Garage was Microsoft’s Xbox Adaptive Controller. The accessibility-focused Xbox controller was a collective effort by employees across Xbox and Surface, but it originated at a hackathon event where employees were experimenting with building a gaming device that used Kinect motion-sensing technology to track movements and translate them to an Xbox controller. An executive saw the nearly 40-person team trying to build the project, turned it into a real thing, and eventually more than 80 employees were involved with bringing the Xbox Adaptive Controller to life. While the device was nearly cut due to budget constraints, it eventually launched and went on to become the star of Microsoft’s 2019 Super Bowl commercial. Microsoft is now planning to wind down its Garage locations, and some spaces will be closed as soon as tomorrow, Friday, October 23rd. The closure of The Garage will also mean changes to Microsoft’s annual employee hackathon event, which could potentially disappear. “As we look to the future, the hackathon team is reimagining the program to meet the needs of today’s employees, customers, and technology landscape. We’ll have more to share at a later date,” says Microsoft’s internal FAQ. Internally, the company is trying to sell employees on the idea that “the spirit of experimentation that once lived primarily in dedicated programs is now reflected in how teams work every day.” Employees I’ve spoken to see the closure as the latest in Microsoft’s continued cutbacks. Earlier this year Microsoft closed its employee library and cut back on subscriptions in favor of an “AI-powered learning experience.” The library used to house thousands of books, journals, and reports that employees could use to learn, research, and explore ideas — much like The Garage. “We’re grateful to the employees, volunteers, and partners who helped build The Garage and look forward to continuing its legacy in new forms,” says Microsoft’s FAQ. It’s hard to imagine anything replicating the unique mix of expert advisers, dedicated maker spaces, hands-on workshops, and internship programs that The Garage offered employees looking to develop new skills. The pad * Microsoft employee causes an Xbox AI stir. Microsoft employee Brandon Stirrup posted multiple times on X this week to get everyone talking about AI use in gaming. “Gaming is the only industry where leaders are afraid to talk about AI,” said Stirrup. “Users want the truth. We’re using AI.” Stirrup’s posts elicited the usual response from gamers against AI, but he said he’s “happy to take the hit if it means hundreds at Xbox can stop pretending that they’re not using AI.” Hours after Stirrup’s posts, he disabled his X account. * Microsoft’s new Photos app combines your PC, OneDrive, and iCloud galleries. Microsoft has redesigned its Photos app for Windows 11, combining images and videos from your PC, OneDrive, and iCloud into a single space. The new app includes a redesigned viewer, a native editor, and a new gallery view. The new editor is the most interesting aspect to me personally, simply because it loads a lot faster now and lets you quickly crop and edit photos. You can also edit HDR, HEIC, and WebP photos. The viewer has also been sped up, with improved HDR viewing and better file type support. * Microsoft says Windows 11 is now “more responsive” and runs better on 8GB of RAM. Microsoft’s fixes for Windows 11 have made it “up to 20 percent more responsive,” according to the company. Microsoft has made improvements to Start, File Explorer, Search, Edge, and other parts of Windows 11 to make the OS feel faster. A big part of the improvements comes down to better memory management, to the point where there is now a “meaningful difference” on PCs with just 8GB of RAM. I still think there is still a way to go to fully improve Windows 11, but these are great first steps compared to a year ago. * Ikea’s Xbox collection is now available online. The new nine-piece “Yxstaby” collection from Ikea was designed in collaboration with Microsoft. It debuted first at Ikea’s physical stores earlier this month, and it’s now available to order online. The line includes accessories and furniture inspired by Xbox controllers. * Nvidia’s latest GPU driver brings a new way to speed up PC games. Nvidia has rolled out a new GPU driver (621.01) this week that enables Microsoft’s new Advanced Shader Delivery technology to speed up game launches. The technology also removes mid-game “just-in-time” shader compilation, reducing stuttering and CPU spikes. Microsoft’s Advanced Shader Delivery works by offloading shader compilation for different hardware combinations to the cloud. Gears of War: E-Day and Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 now both support Advanced Shader Delivery, as long as you download the games via the Xbox PC app. “This system is storefront-agnostic, meaning you benefit even when playing games purchased on Steam, as long as the Xbox PC app is installed on your PC,” says Nvidia’s Andrew Burnes. * Microsoft donated $10 million to Trump’s ballroom. The Washington Post has obtained a list of all the major donors to Donald Trump’s White House ballroom project, including previously undisclosed contributors. Microsoft donated $10 million, which puts it roughly in the middle set of tech donations from the likes of Apple ($25 million), Amazon ($5 million), Nvidia ($25 million), Google ($22 million), and Meta ($5 million). * Xbox mandates a four-day return to office. Microsoft asked its employees to return to the office three days per week last year, and it’s now upping this requirement to four days a week for most Xbox employees. An internal memo, seen by The Verge, describes the change as a “need to create more opportunities for people to work together” after feedback from Xbox employees. “Starting February 1st, 2027, Xbox employees in Puget Sound who live within 50 commuting miles of Studio D are required to work from the office a minimum of four days a week,” says Jacinda Chislum Pearson, Xbox chief people officer, in the internal memo. Some Xbox employees I’ve spoken to view this as a stealth layoff, while others have noted that the existing three-day rule was only lightly enforced. * Microsoft says it’s working on making Edge updates less of a hassle. Microsoft has shared a prototype demo for “seamless updates” to Edge that would avoid you needing to restart the browser. The feature is still in development, but it could certainly help with things like insecure TLS certificates and other issues where a browser needs to be patched. * Surface Laptop Ultra review: a different kind of MacBook Pro. I spent a week reviewing Microsoft’s latest Surface laptop, and I’m impressed with the hardware. The MacBook Pro-esque design is unlike any other Windows laptop, thanks to a large haptic trackpad and USB-C magnetic charging. The software that the Surface Laptop Ultra is trying to push, in particular local AI, feels a lot less polished, though. Overall, the Laptop Ultra is targeted at a very niche audience of AI developers. * Microsoft reportedly plans Xbox handheld in 2027, next-gen console in 2028. Microsoft is reportedly planning to launch an Xbox “next-generation handheld device” for the holiday season of 2027. The Xbox next-gen console, codenamed Project Helix, would then launch in the holidays of 2028, according to a new report from Fortune. It’s not clear if the rumored handheld is an actual first-party Xbox device, or one from an OEM like Asus. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has previously described Project Helix as a “family of devices,” suggesting that Microsoft’s next Xbox console may not be just one piece of hardware. The report also suggests that Sharma is planning a fresh round of Xbox layoffs this month, followed by more in November and January. * Microsoft abandons the UK’s largest data center project. Microsoft is walking away from a deal with Nscale for a new data center in Loughton, Essex. Nscale has faced delays getting the data center online, with UK National Grid officials not able to supply power to the site until the 2030s, according to Reuters. The deal was originally announced ahead of Trump’s second state visit to the UK last year, with Microsoft boasting of its $30 billion investment in the UK. * AMD is bringing FSR 4.1 to Xbox consoles and handhelds. AMD has revealed that it’s bringing its latest upscaling technology, FSR 4.1, to the Xbox Series S and X consoles, as well as laptops, 6000-series GPUs, and both the Xbox Ally and Xbox Ally X handhelds. It’s coming to Xbox developers “very soon,” but Xbox console owners will have to wait a little longer. The frame rate-boosting technology should have a noticeable impact on the Xbox Series S, and it works with more than 300 games, including Cyberpunk 2077, Battlefield 6, and Assassin’s Creed Shadows. * Microsoft: Frontier models cannot be trusted. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said earlier this month that we should assume that all AI models are “compromised,” and now Microsoft is going one step further. “Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted,” says Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security. Microsoft is naturally positioning its new Project Perception as a solution to securing AI models. It’s an agentic security system designed to help cybersecurity professionals secure and control AI agents. * Xbox is experimenting with a blades dashboard. Xbox CTO Scott Van Vliet has been “cooking up retro vibes” as part of Microsoft’s new Xbox Labs effort. The result is what looks like a vibe-coded option to pick your dashboard on an Xbox console. This is simply an experiment right now and it’s not clear if we’ll ever see such an option, but Xbox CEO Asha Sharma asks “blades on the web. Do we like this experiment?” * Microsoft’s headcount is down year-over-year. Microsoft’s annual report reveals the company employed around 223,000 people as of June 30th. That’s 5,000 less than the 228,000 people employed in 2025. It’s the first time Microsoft has had a headcount reduction in 10 years, after the gutting of the Nokia phone business in 2015 and 2016. The reduction comes as Microsoft has laid off more than 9,000 employees over the past year. * Xbox Cloud Gaming’s pay-as-you-go option starts at $3.99 for 10 hours. Microsoft announced last month that it will let anyone access Xbox Cloud Gaming in November, without the need to subscribe to Xbox Game Pass. The new pay-as-you-go model will require players to purchase bundles of cloud hours, and now Microsoft is revealing that bundles will start at $3.99 for 10 hours of cloud playtime. If you want 25 hours it’ll cost $7.99, and 50 hours is $11.99. All of these cloud hours will include ad-free cloud gaming, shorter wait times, and higher-quality streaming. I’m always keen to hear from readers, so please drop a comment here, or you can reach me at notepad@theverge.com if you want to discuss anything else. If you’ve heard about any of Microsoft’s secret projects, you can reach me via email at notepad@theverge.com or speak to me confidentially on the Signal messaging app, where I’m tomwarren.01. I’m also tomwarren on Telegram, if you’d prefer to chat there. Thanks for subscribing to Notepad.

articles.title: Bigg Boss 20: Uditi Singh reveals her Top five predictions to Arishfa Khan; Names Gullu, Qazi, Scout, Arishfa and Mahhi
articles.summary: As the game inside the Bigg Boss 20 house gets intense, contestants Uditi Singh and Arishfa Khan were seen guessing the Top 5 of the show.
articles.body: As the game inside the Bigg Boss 20 house gets intense, contestants Uditi Singh and Arishfa Khan were seen guessing the Top 5 of the show. During the live streaming of the show, the two were seen discussing the finalists of the show.A conversation unfolded inside the Bigg Boss 20 house when Uditi shared her top five predictions with Arishfa. Recalling a discussion with Mahhi, Uditi revealed that when asked to predict the contestants who could make it to the top five, she had named Gullu, Qazi, Scout, Arishfa and Mahhi.Uditi clarified that her predictions were based on her observations of the game so far and did not necessarily reflect whom she personally wanted to see in the top five. However, she added that she did wish for Arishfa to make it to the final five, making her prediction a moment of encouragement for her fellow housemate.When Arishfa questioned Uditi about why she considered Scout a strong contender, Uditi explained that his popularity as a gamer and his large fan following could work in his favour. She believed his existing audience made him a strong player in the competition.Talking about Bigg Boss 20, the show recently witnessed Qazi Touqeer mocking Aasif Khan's medical condition. Aasif's wife shared a heartfelt post revealing about, the actor suffering a heart attack at the age of 34. She penned a note on social media on Thursday, "Yes, Aasif had a heart attack. A massive one. At just 34. It breaks my heart that I now have to share his medical reports just to prove what he went through was real. I never imagined something so personal would have to be made public for people to believe him. (sic)"She clarified that when Aasif initially said it was GERD and not a heart attack, it was out of fear, as he was worried that a serious health condition would cost him work."In an industry where opportunities are uncertain, especially without backing, that fear was real", she further wrote.Recalling the challenging time when Aasif was in the ICU, she shared, "I will never forget being told his main coronary artery was completely blocked, the ICU, the stent, or holding my husband as he cried, afraid of losing the future he had dreamed of. Aasif had already lost his father to a heart attack as a child. Surviving one himself brought back that heartbreak and the fear of leaving his own family behind."Expressing disappointment that Aasif's health was turned into a joke, she added, "This has gone beyond criticism. We have faced vile abuse, death threats against Aasif and rape threats against our family. Nothing can justify this.""Bigg Boss is an entertainment reality show. When did entertainment become an excuse for cruelty? When did disagreements become a reason to threaten someone’s life or target their family?", concluded the post.Get the latest TV News, TV Shows and more. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Jillian Michaels urges parents to fight back against Big Tech's 'addictive' grip on kids
articles.summary: Jillian Michaels expressed concerns about screen time for children and called on parents to hold tech companies accountable in Fox Nation's "Toxic 2: A Generation on the Brink."
articles.body: Fitness trainer and media personality Jillian Michaels is urging parents to "keep the pressure on" social media companies, warning about the platforms' allegedly "addictive" algorithms and content. Michaels made the comments during an appearance on "The Faulkner Focus" while promoting her new Fox Nation documentary, "Toxic 2: A Generation on the Brink." Michaels advised parents to limit their children's access to online activities. "You have to do everything you can," Michaels said. "And that means putting parental controls on your kid's phone, period. Take the phone away at night, limit the sites that they can access, have communications with them regularly about the content that they're seeing online. But you also have to be realistic about what they're going to do when they're not with you." CHRIS HANSEN URGES PARENTS TO TEACH CHILDREN ABOUT ONLINE PREDATORS BEFORE ALLOWING INTERNET ACCESS "This is the part where we also have to continue putting pressure on the social media companies to make their algorithms safer for kids," she said. "They created an addictive product, they know it, and we need to keep the pressure on." In the documentary, Michaels examines the risks she says children face in the modern age, including excessive screen time, mental health issues and over-medicalization. "The truth is, a lot of parents probably don't realize the scale of what kids are dealing with today," she said. "From day one, the fragile little bodies and brains of the tiniest and most vulnerable among us are being targeted, treated and toxified from all angles." NATION'S SECOND-LARGEST SCHOOL DISTRICT MOVES TO LIMIT KIDS' SCREEN TIME Michaels is joined by several experts in "Toxic 2: A Generation on the Brink," including psychology researcher Jean Twenge, who argues that individuals who begin using smartphones at an early age are more likely to experience mental health issues later in life. "In some of the best design studies, the heaviest users of social media are about twice as likely to be depressed as lighter non-users," Twenge said. "Even in other studies, you see at least often a 40% or a 50% increase in depression from not using social media to being a heavy user of social media." "Gen Z and Gen Alpha know how bad these technologies can be for them," Twenge added. "They're the ones who came up with phrases like 'chronically online,' which make it sound like a disease, 'brain rot,' that it's bad for your attention span and your focus." FRANCE BECOMES FIRST EU NATION TO BAN SOCIAL MEDIA FOR CHILDREN UNDER 15 Social media companies have faced increasing pressure to be regulated and be held accountable for the potential effects of their platforms. In August, Meta agreed to pay as much as $17.1 billion and implement restrictions on teen accounts to settle claims that it designed Facebook and Instagram to addict children and misled the public about the platforms' safety. Meta denied the allegations. For more on the potential risks personal tech and other issues pose to young children, make sure to watch "Toxic 2: A Generation on the Brink," now streaming on Fox Nation.
